text: Data Structures & Algorithms: Comprehensive Course Notes Course Code: CS-201 | Subject: Fundamentals of Data Structures, Algorithm Analysis, and Complexity Theory Chapter 1: Foundations of Algorithm Analysis & Asymptotic Notation An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions designed to solve a specific computational problem. When evaluating algorithms, we focus on efficiency: Time Complexity (how runtime scales with input size n) and Space Complexity (how memory usage scales). Rather than measuring execution time in seconds—which depends heavily on hardware, compiler optimizations, and processor load—we analyze asymptotic growth using Big-O, Big- Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) notations. Asymptotic Notation Definitions: Big-O (O) - Upper Bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n0. Represents worst-case running time. Big-Omega (Ω) - Lower Bound: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if f(n) ≥ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n0. Represents best-case running time. Big-Theta (Θ) - Tight Bound: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if c1 · g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2 · g(n). Represents exact growth rate. Chapter 2: Linear Data Structures - Arrays & Dynamic Vectors An Array is a contiguous block of memory allocated to store homogeneous elements. Because elements reside sequentially in physical memory, accessing any element by its index i occurs in constant time O(1) via the address formula: Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + i × ElementSize. However, insertions and deletions at arbitrary positions require shifting elements, incurring an O(n) time complexity. Dynamic Arrays (such as C++ `std::vector` or Python `list`) overcome fixed-size constraints by automatically resizing when full. Amortized Complexity Analysis of Doubling Strategy: When capacity doubles at powers of 2, inserting n elements causes copies at steps 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2k. Total copies = ∑i=0 k 2i = 2k+1 - 1 < 2n. Chapter 3: Singly and Doubly Linked Lists A Linked List is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are stored non-contiguously in memory. Each node contains data and a pointer (reference) to the next node. Unlike arrays, linked lists allow O(1) insertions and deletions at known pointer locations without shifting elements. However, random access is impossible; accessing the k-th element requires traversing nodes sequentially in O(k) time. Chapter 4: Stacks, Queues, and Monotonic Variants Stacks follow a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) discipline, while Queues operate on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) basis. Both are abstract data types (ADTs) restricted to specific access points. Stacks support `push`, `pop`, and `peek` operations in O(1) time, making them essential for function call stacks, expression evaluation, and backtracking. Queues support `enqueue` and `dequeue` in O(1) time, operating as buffers for BFS traversals and process scheduling. Chapter 5: Recursion & Divide-and-Conquer Paradigm Recursion is a programming technique where a function solves a problem by calling reduced instances of itself. Every recursive function must define one or more base cases (stopping conditions) and a recursive step that moves toward the base case. Unbounded recursion results in stack overflow errors due to call stack memory exhaustion. The Divide-and-Conquer paradigm breaks a problem into disjoint subproblems, recursively solves them, and combines their solutions. The Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer Recurrences: For recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), where a ≥ 1, b > 1: Case 1: If f(n) = O(nlogba - ε), then T(n) = Θ(nlogba). Case 2: If f(n) = Θ(nlogba logk n), then T(n) = Θ(nlogba logk+1 n). Case 3: If f(n) = Ω(nlogba + ε) and regularity holds, then T(n) = Θ(f(n)). Quiz Benchmark Questions: 1. Apply the Master Theorem to solve T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n. Identify values for a, b, and the matching case. 2. Chapter 6: Sorting Algorithms - Comparison & Non-Comparison Sorting arranges elements in a specified order. Comparison-based algorithms have a lower bound proof of Ω(n log n) time complexity. Quadratic algorithms (O(n2)) like Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort are inefficient for large inputs, whereas Merge Sort and Quick Sort achieve O(n log n). Non-comparison sorts (Counting Sort, Radix Sort) break the Ω(n log n) barrier by exploiting key distribution properties. Chapter 7: Trees & Binary Search Trees (BST) A Tree is a hierarchical non-linear data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. A Binary Tree restricts each node to at most two children (left and right). A Binary Search Tree (BST) enforces the structural property: for any node X, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than X.key, and all keys in the right subtree are strictly greater. Inorder traversal of a BST yields elements in sorted ascending order. Chapter 8: Self-Balancing Trees (AVL) & Heaps To prevent BST degradation to linear linked lists (O(n) search), self-balancing trees enforce height invariants. An AVL Tree requires that for every node, the height difference between left and right subtrees (Balance Factor) is at most ±1: BF = Height(Left) - Height(Right) ∈ {-1, 0, 1}. Violations trigger rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL). A Binary Heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property: Max-Heap (Parent ≥ Child) or Min-Heap (Parent ≤ Child). AVL Tree Rotation Rules summary: Single Left Rotation (RR Insertion): Applied when a right child's right subtree causes imbalance. Single Right Rotation (LL Insertion): Applied when a left child's left subtree causes imbalance. Double Rotation (LR / RL Insertion): Performed as a combination of sub-tree single rotation followed by root rotation. Quiz Benchmark Questions: 1. Chapter 9: Hash Tables & Collision Resolution A Hash Table maps keys to values using a Hash Function h(k), computing array indices in average O(1) time. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across slots. When two keys map to the same index (h(k1) = h(k2)), a Collision occurs. The two primary collision resolution techniques are Separate Chaining (linked lists per bucket) and Open Addressing (probing contiguous memory slots). Open Addressing Probing Techniques: Linear Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) mod m. Simple, but suffers from Primary Clustering. Quadratic Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c1i + c2i2) mod m. Reduces primary clustering. Double Hashing: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i · h2(k)) mod m. Eliminates secondary clustering. Quiz Benchmark Questions: 1. Given a hash table of size 10 using h(k) = k mod 10 and Linear Probing, insert keys `12, 22, 32, 42`. State the final array index for each key. 2. What is the Load Factor (α) of a hash table, and at what threshold should resizing (rehashing) be triggered to maintain O(1) operations? CS-201: Data Structures & Algorithms Page 9 of 10

Chapter 10: Graph Algorithms - BFS, DFS & Shortest Paths A Graph G = (V, E) consists of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections), which can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Graphs are represented using Adjacency Matrices (O(V2) space, fast edge lookup) or Adjacency Lists (O(V + E) space, preferred for sparse graphs). Graph traversals underpin routing protocols, social network analysis, and topological sorting.
